summary: Updates the specification of the IPv4 Identification field. The old rule required uniqueness for every datagram, which would limit connections to about 6.4 Mbps for typical sizes, so this document relaxes it for cases where fragmentation is not used, and updates related rules.

plainLanguage.summary: Every package got a one-of-a-kind number, but fast delivery runs out of numbers. This relaxes the rule when a package is not going to be split up.

questions: what is the ipv4 id field used for
does the ipv4 identification field need to be unique
why is ipv4 id uniqueness limited to 6.4 mbps
subtitle: The IPv4 ID field only has to be unique when a packet might be fragmented; otherwise its value means nothing.

tldr.problem: IPv4 required the 16-bit ID field to be unique for every datagram within the maximum datagram lifetime. Strictly enforced, that would cap a connection at 6.4 Mbps for typical datagram sizes, so real systems already break the rule.
tldr.mechanism: The ID is defined only for fragmentation and reassembly. Datagrams that cannot be fragmented (atomic datagrams) may use any ID, and everything that reads IPv4 headers must ignore it for them. Uniqueness is kept for datagrams that are or may be fragmented.
tldr.outcome: The specification now matches practice and is closer to IPv6. It updates RFC 791, RFC 1122 and RFC 2003.

today: RFC 6864 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2013. It updates RFC 791, RFC 1122 and RFC 2003, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with a Unique ID
sections.content:
In IPv4 the Identification (ID) field is a 16-bit value that, by the old rules in RFC 791 and RFC 1122, is unique for every datagram for a given source address, destination address and protocol, so that it does not repeat within the maximum datagram lifetime (MDL). The MDL is typically interpreted as two minutes. The old rule applied regardless of fragmentation settings.

High-speed devices commonly violate this. If it were strictly enforced, it would limit a single protocol between two IP endpoints to 6.4 Mbps for typical MTUs of 1500 bytes, using the analysis in RFC 4963. Some sources have also sent non-varying IDs for years, for example cellphones, which led to support for that in RObust Header Compression (RFC 5225).

This document updates the specification to match current practice and the considerations behind the similar field in IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule said every parcel needs its own number, but fast senders break that rule all the time and nothing bad seems to happen. So the rule was rewritten to match what really happens.

sections.title: How the ID Field Is Used
sections.content:
Fragmentation splits a large datagram into pieces to cross links with a small MTU. In IPv4 the pieces are marked by four header fields: ID, Fragment Offset, the Don't Fragment (DF) flag and the More Fragments (MF) flag. Fragments of one original datagram are matched by their ID within a source, destination and protocol.

In IPv6, fragmentation occurs only at the source, the ID sits in a fragment extension header that is present only when the datagram is fragmented (with one translation case), and the ID is 32 bits. IPv6 acts as if DF=1 always.

Other uses of the IPv4 ID have been proposed, such as detecting duplicate datagrams (noted in RFC 1122) and correlating datagrams in diagnostic tools. These uses are deprecated here.

The arithmetic: with a 16-bit ID that does not repeat within 120 seconds and the maximum IPv4 datagram size of 64 KB, the aggregate of connections between two endpoints is limited to roughly 286 Mbps, dropping to 6.4 Mbps at a 1500-byte MTU. IPv6 with its larger ID can reach 18.7 Tbps with fragmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: When a big parcel is cut into pieces, the pieces carry the same number so the receiver can glue the right ones together. Only that job really needs the number.

sections.title: Atomic and Non-atomic Datagrams
sections.content:
The document splits datagrams into two kinds. Atomic datagrams are not yet fragmented and have further fragmentation inhibited. Non-atomic datagrams have either already been fragmented or can still be fragmented.

The test uses only header fields, so it is backward compatible and no ID value, including 0, is reserved as special. Every datagram is exactly one of the two kinds.
sections.plainLanguage: An atomic datagram is a parcel marked "do not cut" that is still in one piece. Anything else might be cut up or already is.

sections.title: The New Rules
sections.content:
The RFC marks its requirements with >> in the text. The main ones are:

  • The IPv4 ID field MUST NOT be used for purposes other than fragmentation and reassembly.
  • Originating sources MAY set the ID of atomic datagrams to any value.
  • All devices that examine IPv4 headers MUST ignore the ID of atomic datagrams.
  • The ID of a non-atomic datagram MUST NOT be reused when sending a copy of an earlier non-atomic datagram.
  • Sources emitting non-atomic datagrams MUST NOT repeat ID values within one MDL for a given source, destination and protocol. This keeps the uniqueness rule from RFC 791 for them.
  • Datagrams with DF=1 MUST NOT be fragmented, and transit devices MUST NOT clear the DF bit.

Duplicate detection can still be done without the ID, using hash-based methods as in RFC 6621. Receivers still need to support overlapping fragments, since in-network duplication can still cause them.
sections.plainLanguage: If a parcel cannot be cut up, its number does not matter and nobody should look at it. If it can be cut, its number must stay unique for a while and must never be reused for a resend.

sections.title: Sources, Middleboxes and Compression
sections.content:
Sources of non-atomic datagrams MUST rate-limit their output to comply with the uniqueness requirement; the RFC names DNS over UDP as an example. Because the MDL has no strict definition, higher-layer protocols SHOULD check integrity with a checksum or hash that can detect reassembly errors (the UDP and TCP checksums are weak but better than nothing). Sources using strong integrity checks MAY reuse the ID within intervals smaller than typical MDL values.

Address-sharing and rewriting devices, such as NATs and tunnel ingresses, count as datagram sources. They MUST make the ID of translated datagrams comply as if they had sourced them, rather than copying it from the incoming datagram.

Header compression schemes already handle IDs that change in various ways. Where compression can assume a non-changing ID, as with ROHC and ECRTP, efficiency can increase; where it assumes a changing ID, a constant ID can make compression less efficient.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who relabels parcels in transit must give them proper numbers, as if they had sent them. Senders who cut parcels should also add a check that catches pieces glued together wrongly.

sections.title: Impact on Existing Devices
sections.content:
The RFC argues the change is low-risk because the behavior already exists. Devices already reuse IDs sooner than the two-minute estimate, some cellphones send non-varying IDs for atomic datagrams, and RFC 6145 also describes generating IPv4 datagrams with constant (zero) IDs. No adverse effects from this have been reported.

Devices that fragment while ignoring DF are non-compliant. If fragments of different datagrams with the same ID arrive interleaved at the destination, reassembly would fail and traffic would be dropped, but significant reassembly errors have not been reported. The RFC adds that it would be more productive to fix such devices than to define specifications that tolerate them.

Duplicate-detection and diagnostic mechanisms should use IPv6-compatible methods that do not rely on the ID.
sections.plainLanguage: Many devices already ignore the old rule and the world has not fallen over, so writing the new rule down mostly just tells the truth.

sections.title: What It Changes in Earlier RFCs
sections.content:
The document updates three RFCs.

  • RFC 791: ID uniqueness applies only to non-atomic datagrams, and retransmitted non-atomic datagrams may no longer reuse the ID. RFC 791 had suggested that TCP might retransmit with the same identifier.
  • RFC 1122: the ID may no longer be used for duplicate detection, for atomic or non-atomic datagrams, and retransmitted non-atomic datagrams may not reuse the ID. RFC 1122 had said a host MAY retain the same ID in an identical copy.
  • RFC 2003: the ID of the outer header of IPv4-in-IPv4 tunnels is set as permitted by RFC 6864.
sections.plainLanguage: Three older rulebooks each get a small edit so that they agree with the new rule.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the ID of atomic datagrams is ignored on receipt, its value is unconstrained and can more easily be used as a covert channel. For some atomic datagrams it may be desirable to rewrite the ID to avoid that. Rewriting would be prohibited for datagrams protected by the IPsec Authentication Header, although the RFC does not recommend using AH to achieve this.

The ID also adds much less entropy to the header, though IDs were never assured of enough entropy for cryptographic use. Finally, dropping uniqueness for atomic datagrams can defeat the ability to count devices behind a NAT, which the RFC says is not intended as a security feature.
sections.plainLanguage: A number that nobody checks could be used to sneak secret messages, so some devices might scramble it. It also stops people from counting how many computers sit behind a shared address.
